Not everything can be responded to. Summoning a monster, Tributing, changing a battle position, and paying a cost are not activations — you cannot start a chain in response to them. You can only chain to the activation of a card or effect.

🔗Spell Speed 1, 2, and 3

Every effect has a Spell Speed from 1 to 3. To respond to a link, your effect must be Spell Speed 2 or higher and at least as fast as the link you are answering.

  • Spell Speed 1 (slowest) — Normal, Equip, Continuous, Field, and Ritual Spells; and monster Ignition, Trigger, and Flip effects. These cannot be activated in response to anything, so they are normally Chain Link 1 (unless several trigger at once).
  • Spell Speed 2 — Normal and Continuous Trap Cards, Quick-Play Spells, and monster Quick Effects. These can respond to Spell Speed 1 or 2, and can usually be activated in any phase — including your opponent's turn.
  • Spell Speed 3 (fastest) — Counter Trap Cards. These can respond to any Spell Speed, and only another Spell Speed 3 can respond to them.

🔗How a chain resolves: last in, first out

A chain resolves in reverse order — this is often called last-in-first-out (LIFO). The last Chain Link added resolves first, then the one below it, and so on, with Chain Link 1 resolving last.

Example. You activate Heavy Storm (Spell Speed 1) as Chain Link 1. Your opponent responds with Threatening Roar (Spell Speed 2) as Chain Link 2. You respond with Seven Tools of the Bandit (Spell Speed 3) as Chain Link 3. It resolves 3 → 2 → 1: Seven Tools negates Threatening Roar, so Threatening Roar does nothing, and then Heavy Storm resolves and destroys the Spell/Trap Cards.

🔗Targeting and costs

Some effects target — you choose the specific card(s) affected when you activate the effect, so both players know the target and can decide whether to respond. Effects that hit "all" cards, or that pick a card only as they resolve, do not target.

A cost (discarding, paying Life Points, Tributing, banishing) is paid when you activate the effect, before it goes on the chain. You do not get the cost back even if the effect is later negated. Edison has a specific rule about Life Point costs that would drop you to 0 — see Rule #10 — Life Point Costs.

🔗When you get to respond

The turn player acts first in each phase and step. The opponent can respond once the turn player passes priority. You respond to an activation, not to a Summon, a position change, or a cost. On top of this base rule, Edison gives the turn player an extra window right after a Summon — see Rule #6 — Ignition Effect Priority.

🔗Simultaneous effects

Sometimes several effects trigger at the same moment. They do not each get their own chain — they are ordered into one chain by a set procedure (broadly: the turn player's effects go on first, then the opponent's, so the opponent's resolve first). Edison uses a specific step-by-step ordering with an era quirk — see Rule #7 — Simultaneous Effects Go On Chain (SEGOC).

meta.title: Building a Deck
meta.summary: An Edison deck is a Main Deck of 40–60 cards, an Extra Deck of 0–15 (Fusion and Synchro only), and a Side Deck of 0–15, with at most 3 copies of any card by name — fewer if the March 2010 banlist marks it Forbidden (0), Limited (1), or Semi-Limited (2).

rules.primer.deck.html:
TL;DR: A legal deck is a Main Deck of 40–60, an Extra Deck of 0–15 (Fusion and Synchro only), and a Side Deck of 0–15. You may run at most 3 copies of any card by name — unless the March 2010 banlist marks it Forbidden (0), Limited (1), or Semi-Limited (2).

🔗Main Deck

Your Main Deck must be 40 to 60 cards. It holds your Monster, Spell, and Trap Cards — including Ritual Monsters, which live in the Main Deck. Most players stay near the 40-card minimum so they draw their best cards more consistently.

🔗Extra Deck

Your Extra Deck may hold 0 to 15 cards, and in this era it contains only Fusion Monsters and Synchro Monsters. Extra Deck cards do not count toward the 40-card Main Deck minimum. (For how these monsters reach the field, see the summoning primer.)

🔗Side Deck

Your Side Deck may hold 0 to 15 cards. It is a separate set of cards used to adjust your deck between duels in a match: after a duel you may swap cards one-for-one between your Side Deck and your Main Deck and/or Extra Deck. The Side Deck's size is fixed across the match — after swapping, it must contain exactly the same number of cards as before. You show your opponent the count (not the contents).

🔗Copy limits

You may include at most 3 copies of any one card by name, counted across your Main Deck, Extra Deck, and Side Deck combined. Cards with the same name are treated as the same card, so three copies is the cap even if the artwork differs.

🔗The banlist

Some cards are restricted further by the banlist (the Forbidden & Limited List). There are three levels:

  • Forbidden — 0 copies allowed; the card cannot be used at all.
  • Limited — at most 1 copy.
  • Semi-Limited — at most 2 copies.

Edison format uses the March 2010 TCG Forbidden & Limited List. That specific list is a defining part of the format — it is what keeps the power level frozen to early 2010. The app's deck builder enforces these limits for you and flags anything illegal.

meta.title: How a Turn Works
meta.summary: Every turn runs through six phases in a fixed order — Draw, Standby, Main Phase 1, Battle, Main Phase 2, End — and the player who goes first draws a card but cannot attack on turn 1.

rules.primer.turn.html:
TL;DR: A turn always runs through six phases in the same order — Draw ▸ Standby ▸ Main Phase 1 ▸ Battle ▸ Main Phase 2 ▸ End. Players start with 8000 Life Points and a 5-card hand; the goal is to drop the opponent to 0. The player who goes first draws on turn 1 but cannot attack on turn 1.

This page teaches the shape of a turn in Edison format, which runs on the 2008–2010 rules (Master Rule 1). If you already know modern Yu-Gi-Oh, most of this is familiar — the two things Edison does differently on turn 1 are called out below and in the 13 rule-differences.

🔗Who goes first

Before the first duel, both players shuffle, then use a coin toss, die roll, or rock-paper-scissors to decide who chooses. The winner picks whether to go first or second ("play or draw"). In the later duels of a match, the loser of the previous duel makes that choice. A match is best two-out-of-three duels.

Both players then draw a 5-card opening hand and start with 8000 Life Points.

Example. You win the die roll and choose to go first. You and your opponent each draw 5 cards, and you take the first turn.

🔗The six phases

Each turn moves through these phases in this exact order:

  • Draw Phase (DP) — draw 1 card.
  • Standby Phase (SP) — resolve effects that happen "during the Standby Phase."
  • Main Phase 1 (MP1) — Summon, Set, and activate most of your cards.
  • Battle Phase (BP) — declare attacks (optional).
  • Main Phase 2 (MP2) — like Main Phase 1; only happens if you conducted a Battle Phase.
  • End Phase (EP) — clean-up and hand-size discard.

You do not have to use every phase. The Battle Phase is optional, and if you conduct no battles you go straight from Main Phase 1 to the End Phase (skipping Main Phase 2).

🔗Draw Phase

The turn player draws 1 card from the top of their Deck. A player who must draw but has no cards left in their Deck loses the duel (this is called decking out). After drawing, players may still activate Trap Cards or Quick-Play Spells before moving on.

🔗Standby Phase

A quiet phase used to resolve effects and pay costs that specifically happen "during the Standby Phase" (for example, some maintenance costs). If nothing applies, play passes straight to Main Phase 1.

🔗Main Phase 1

This is where most of the game happens. During Main Phase 1 you can:

  • Normal Summon or Set one monster (once per turn).
  • Change the battle position of your face-up monsters (with some restrictions).
  • Activate Spell, Trap, and monster effects.
  • Set Spell and Trap Cards face-down.
  • Special Summon monsters (Synchro, Fusion, Ritual, and by card effects) as often as their conditions allow.

For all the ways to put a monster on the field, see the summoning primer.

🔗Battle Phase

If you want to attack, you enter the Battle Phase. It has its own steps (Start, Battle, Damage, End) and is where battle damage is calculated. This page only flags when the Battle Phase happens in the turn — the full mechanics (attack declaration, the Damage Step, and replays) are covered in the Battle Phase primer.

🔗Main Phase 2

After a Battle Phase, you return to a Main Phase. Main Phase 2 works exactly like Main Phase 1, except you cannot repeat a once-per-turn action you already used — so if you Normal Summoned in Main Phase 1, you cannot Normal Summon again here. Use it to set up your defenses for the opponent's turn.

🔗End Phase

Announce the end of your turn. Effects that say "during the End Phase" resolve now. Then, if you are holding more than 6 cards, you must discard down to a hand size of 6.

Example. You finish your turn holding 8 cards. During your End Phase you discard 2, ending with 6.

🔗The first player draws on turn 1

In Edison, the player who goes first does draw during their very first Draw Phase. So going first, you begin your first Main Phase with 6 cards (5 opening cards + 1 drawn). This is different from modern Yu-Gi-Oh, where the first player skips their turn-1 draw. See Rule #1 — The Starting Player Draws a Card.

🔗The first player cannot attack on turn 1

The player who goes first cannot conduct a Battle Phase on their very first turn — there are no first-turn attacks. Attacks become available from that player's second turn onward. (The player going second may attack normally on their first turn.)

Example. You go first and Summon a 1900-ATK monster. You still cannot attack this turn; your Battle Phase is skipped. Your opponent, going second, could attack on their first turn.

🔗Who acts first: priority

Within each phase and step, the turn player acts first — this is called having priority. While the turn player holds priority, the opponent cannot activate cards, except for effects that trigger automatically. The turn player either uses priority to do something, or passes it; passing lets the opponent respond, and it passes automatically when you move to the next phase or step.

Edison adds one extra priority rule on top of this: after a Summon, the turn player can get to act before the opponent — see Rule #6 — Ignition Effect Priority. For how responses stack up into a chain, see the chains and Spell Speed primer.

meta.title: Summoning Monsters
meta.summary: There are several ways to put monsters on the field — Normal Summon or Set (once per turn, with Tributes for higher Levels), Flip Summon, and Special Summons such as Synchro, Fusion, and Ritual — and the Extra Deck this era holds only Fusion and Synchro Monsters.

rules.primer.summoning.html:
TL;DR: You may Normal Summon or Set one monster per turn (higher-Level monsters cost Tributes). Everything else — Flip Summon, and the Special Summons (Synchro, Fusion, Ritual, and card-effect summons) — has no per-turn cap beyond each card's own conditions. This era's Extra Deck holds only Fusion and Synchro Monsters.

🔗Normal Summon and Tribute Summon

A Normal Summon plays a monster from your hand onto the field in face-up Attack Position. You may Normal Summon or Set only once per turn (in either Main Phase). Higher-Level monsters require you to Tribute (send to the Graveyard) monsters you control first:

  • Level 1–4 — no Tribute.
  • Level 5–6 — Tribute 1 monster.
  • Level 7 or higher — Tribute 2 monsters.

A Normal Summon that needs Tributes is called a Tribute Summon. It still uses up your one Normal-Summon-or-Set for the turn.

Example. You Tribute one monster you control to Normal Summon a Level 6 monster. That is your Normal Summon for the turn.

🔗Set

To Set a monster is to play it from your hand in face-down Defense Position. A Set monster is not considered Summoned yet — it is hidden, and its effects generally do nothing until it is face-up. Setting a Level 5+ monster still costs the appropriate Tributes, and Setting uses your one Normal-Summon-or-Set for the turn.

🔗Flip Summon

A Flip Summon turns one of your face-down Defense Position monsters face-up into Attack Position, without using a card effect. You can Flip Summon as many monsters as you like per turn, but not a monster on the same turn you Set it. Flipping a monster face-up activates any Flip Effect it has.

🔗Special Summon

A Special Summon puts a monster on the field without using your Normal Summon or Set. It happens through a card's effect, or through a monster's own Summoning condition (for example, Cyber Dragon Special Summons itself when your opponent controls a monster and you do not). Special Summoned monsters enter in your choice of face-up Attack Position or face-up Defense Position, and you may perform as many as the cards allow.

Synchro, Fusion, and Ritual Summons (below) are all Special Summons.

After a Special Summon that does not start a chain, the turn player can act before the opponent responds — this is Edison's Ignition Effect Priority. See Rule #6 — Ignition Effect Priority.

🔗Synchro Summon (and Tuners)

Synchro Summoning is the signature mechanic of this era. You Special Summon a Synchro Monster from the Extra Deck by sending, from your side of the field to the Graveyard, 1 face-up Tuner monster plus one or more face-up non-Tuner monsters whose Levels add up to exactly the Synchro Monster's Level. A Tuner is any monster with "Tuner" printed in its type line. There is no Rank or Xyz mechanic in this era.

Example. You control Junk Synchron (a Level 3 Tuner) and Speed Warrior (Level 2). 3 + 2 = 5, so you send both to the Graveyard and Synchro Summon a Level 5 Synchro Monster from your Extra Deck.

🔗Fusion Summon

A Fusion Summon brings out a Fusion Monster from the Extra Deck. Normally you activate Polymerization, send the specific Fusion Material Monsters listed on the Fusion Monster (from your hand or field) to the Graveyard, and Special Summon the Fusion Monster. Some cards perform a Fusion Summon with their own effect instead of Polymerization.

🔗Ritual Summon

A Ritual Summon uses a Ritual Spell Card together with the matching Ritual Monster (which lives in your Main Deck, not the Extra Deck). You activate the Ritual Spell and Tribute monsters whose Levels meet the requirement printed on the Ritual Spell, then Special Summon the Ritual Monster.

Example. You activate the Ritual Spell "End of the World," Tribute monsters totalling the required Levels, and Ritual Summon Demise, King of Armageddon.

🔗The Extra Deck: Fusion and Synchro only

Synchro and Fusion Monsters do not go in your Main Deck — they live in your separate Extra Deck. In Edison, the Extra Deck contains only Fusion Monsters and Synchro Monsters. The later Extra-Deck types — Xyz (Rank), Pendulum, and Link — were introduced after this era and are not part of Edison. For deck sizes and limits, see the deck-building primer.
